clinicalPearls: Peripheral nerve injuries are graded by severity using the Seddon classification of neurapraxia, axonotmesis, and neurotmesis, and the more detailed Sunderland scheme, which together guide prognosis and management

Neurapraxia is a conduction block with intact axons that usually recovers fully; axonotmesis involves axonal disruption with preserved connective tissue framework and slow recovery; neurotmesis is complete transection that generally requires surgical repair
Clinical assessment maps motor, sensory, and autonomic deficits to the affected nerve and helps localise the lesion and estimate its completeness
Electrodiagnostic studies are most informative after a few weeks, once Wallerian degeneration is established, and are useful for confirming the lesion, grading severity, and tracking reinnervation
Rehabilitation emphasises preventing complications during recovery: maintaining joint range of motion, protective splinting, skin care in insensate areas, and preventing contracture and disuse
An advancing Tinel sign along the nerve over successive examinations is a helpful bedside indicator of regenerating axons
Axonal regrowth proceeds slowly at roughly a millimetre per day, so recovery of distal muscles can take many months and the muscle must remain viable for reinnervation to be useful

Neuropathic pain following nerve injury is managed with neuropathic agents such as gabapentinoids and antidepressants alongside therapy, and surgical exploration or nerve transfer is considered when there is no recovery within the expected window
reference.pathophysiology: Peripheral nerve injury disrupts axonal continuity and myelin to varying degrees depending on the mechanism, whether compression, traction, laceration, or ischaemia. In neurapraxia there is focal demyelination and conduction block without axonal loss. When axons are disrupted, the segment distal to the injury undergoes Wallerian degeneration, and regeneration then proceeds from the proximal stump along preserved endoneurial tubes, guided by Schwann cells and neurotrophic signals. The integrity of the connective tissue sheaths determines whether regrowing axons reach their correct targets; disrupted architecture leads to misdirection, neuroma formation, and incomplete recovery.
additionalDifferentials: Entrapment neuropathy such as carpal or cubital tunnel syndrome
Motor neuron disease or other central cause of weakness
Compartment syndrome affecting nerve and muscle
additionalInvestigations: Detailed motor and sensory examination to localise and grade the lesion
Nerve conduction studies and electromyography, timed appropriately after injury to assess severity and reinnervation
Serial examination for an advancing Tinel sign as evidence of regeneration
Imaging such as ultrasound or MRI to define nerve continuity and identify compression or neuroma
Assessment for coexisting vascular or musculoskeletal injury in trauma
redFlags: Suspected complete nerve transection or a sharp penetrating injury that may need early surgical exploration and repair
Signs of compartment syndrome in an acutely painful, tense limb
Rapidly progressive or multifocal deficits suggesting a systemic or inflammatory neuropathy
Vascular compromise accompanying the nerve injury
No sign of recovery within the expected timeframe, warranting reassessment for surgery
reference.prognosis: Prognosis depends chiefly on the injury grade: neurapraxia typically recovers fully within weeks to months, axonotmesis recovers slowly and often incompletely, and neurotmesis requires surgical repair with outcomes limited by the distance to the target and the age of the patient. More proximal injuries and delayed treatment carry a poorer outlook because muscle may atrophy irreversibly before reinnervation occurs.
pitfalls: Performing electrodiagnostic studies too early, before Wallerian degeneration makes findings interpretable
Missing a transection that requires timely surgical repair
Allowing contractures and joint stiffness to develop during the long recovery period
Neglecting skin protection in areas rendered insensate by the injury
Failing to reassess and refer for surgery when expected recovery does not occur
management: Repair transected nerves surgically by primary coaptation, nerve grafting or nerve transfer for neurotmesis, ideally in a timely manner to optimise reinnervation
Manage neurapraxia and axonotmesis conservatively with observation, as many recover spontaneously along preserved endoneurial tubes
Prevent secondary complications with joint range-of-motion exercises, protective splinting, skin care of insensate areas and prevention of contracture and disuse
Treat neuropathic pain with agents such as gabapentinoids or tricyclic antidepressants and address a symptomatic neuroma if it develops
Monitor recovery with serial examination for an advancing Tinel sign and with electrodiagnostic studies timed after Wallerian degeneration is established
Provide physical and occupational therapy for functional rehabilitation, escalating to reconstructive options such as tendon transfers if recovery fails
